title: CSS Selectors
subtitle: Learn to Target Exactly What You Want
description: Master CSS selectors and learn how to target HTML elements precisely using element, class, ID, grouping, descendant, child, attribute and combined selectors. Apply these selectors to a realistic dashboard interface.

blocks.text: What Are CSS Selectors?
Welcome to Lesson 2.
In the previous lesson, you learned that CSS needs a way to identify the HTML elements it should style.
Today, we are going to study that part of CSS in much greater detail.
Selectors are one of the most important foundations of CSS.
A selector tells the browser which HTML elements a CSS rule should target.
The better you understand selectors, the more precisely you can control an interface.
Imagine a dashboard containing dozens of buttons, cards, headings, links and paragraphs.
You would not want one CSS rule to accidentally style everything.
You need a way to tell CSS exactly which elements you mean.
That is what selectors allow you to do.
Think of a selector as a targeting system.
The selector identifies the target, and the declarations describe what should happen to that target.

blocks.title: A Simple Selector
blocks.output: Every paragraph targeted by this rule receives the specified text color.

blocks.text: Here, p is the selector.
The selector tells CSS to target paragraph elements.
Now let's learn how to make that targeting more precise.

blocks.question: What is the primary job of a CSS selector?
options: To define the value of a CSS property
To identify which HTML elements a CSS rule targets
To connect JavaScript to a webpage
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A selector identifies the HTML elements that should receive a CSS rule.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about the part of a CSS rule that tells the browser what should be targeted.
blocks.reasoning: Selectors identify the elements that CSS declarations should be applied to.

blocks.text: Element Selectors
Let's begin with the simplest type of selector.
It is called an element selector.
An element selector uses the name of an HTML element.

blocks.title: Element Selector Examples
blocks.output:
h1 elements receive the heading size.
p elements receive the text color.
button elements receive the padding.

blocks.text: The h1 selector targets h1 elements.
The p selector targets paragraph elements.
The button selector targets button elements.
There is something important to notice here.
If your page contains several paragraphs, a p selector can target all of them.
That can be useful when every paragraph should share the same basic styling.
But it becomes a problem when only some paragraphs should look different.
That is when we need more specific selectors.

blocks.title: Different Paragraphs
blocks.output: Three paragraph elements appear on the page.

blocks.text: Suppose only the middle paragraph should be highlighted.
A plain p selector would affect all three paragraphs.
We need a way to identify the special paragraph.

blocks.question: What happens when you write p { color: red; }?
options: Only the first paragraph becomes red.
Only paragraphs with a class named p become red.
All targeted p elements receive the red text color.
The p element itself becomes a red HTML tag.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. An element selector targets elements of that type.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Remember that p is the HTML element selector for paragraphs.
blocks.reasoning: A p selector matches paragraph elements, so the declaration can apply to all matching paragraphs.

blocks.text: Class Selectors
Now we are going to solve the problem of styling only selected elements.
The class selector is one of the most useful selectors in real application development.
A class allows you to create a reusable styling category.

blocks.title: Adding Classes
blocks.code:
Welcome to your dashboard.

Your session is about to expire.
blocks.output: The elements now have reusable class names.

blocks.text: The first paragraph has the class description.
The second paragraph has the class warning.
The button has the class primary.
In CSS, a class selector starts with a dot.

blocks.title: Selecting Classes
blocks.output: Each class receives its own styling.

blocks.text: The dot tells CSS that description is a class name.
The same idea applies to warning and primary.
Classes are reusable, so multiple elements can share the same class.

blocks.title: Reusing a Class
blocks.output: All three buttons share the primary class.

blocks.text: One CSS rule can now style all three buttons.
This is one reason classes are so important in large interfaces.
You can design a component once and reuse its styling across your application.

blocks.question: Which CSS selector correctly targets class="primary"?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Class selectors begin with a dot.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Remember that CSS uses a dot to select a class.
blocks.reasoning: .primary targets elements whose class list contains primary.

blocks.text: Multiple Classes on One Element
Now let's look at a powerful feature of classes.
One HTML element can have more than one class.

blocks.title: Combining Classes
blocks.output: The button has three classes: button, primary and large.

blocks.text: The button class could define the general button design.
The primary class could define the main button color.
The large class could define a larger size.

blocks.title: Styling Multiple Classes
blocks.output: The button receives styles from all matching classes.

blocks.text: The browser combines the matching rules when the element has all those classes.
This allows you to build flexible components from small reusable styles.
You do not always need to create a completely new class for every variation.
You can combine a base class with modifier classes.

blocks.question: What does class="button primary large" mean?
options: The element has one class whose name contains spaces.
The element has three separate classes.
Only the last class is applied.
The browser treats the classes as three different HTML elements.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Spaces separate multiple class names in the class attribute.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look carefully at how class names are separated inside the class attribute.
blocks.reasoning: The element has the classes button, primary and large, so rules for each matching class can apply.

blocks.text: ID Selectors
Next, let's examine ID selectors.
An ID gives an element a unique identifier within a document.

blocks.title: Adding an ID
blocks.output: The header has the ID main-header.

blocks.text: In CSS, an ID selector begins with a hash symbol.

blocks.title: Selecting an ID
blocks.output: The element with ID main-header receives the styles.

blocks.text: The selector #main-header targets the element whose ID is main-header.
IDs are useful when you need to identify a particular element.
However, reusable components should generally be styled with classes.
This makes your CSS easier to reuse and maintain.

blocks.question: Which selector targets id="main-header"?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The # symbol identifies an ID selector.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Remember the selector symbol used for IDs.
blocks.reasoning: #main-header specifically targets the element with id="main-header".

blocks.text: Grouping Selectors
Sometimes several different elements need exactly the same style.
Instead of repeating the same declarations in separate rules, you can group selectors.

blocks.title: Grouping Selectors
blocks.output: The same declarations apply to h1, h2 and h3.

blocks.text: The commas separate the selectors.
The declarations after the opening brace are shared by all three selectors.
This reduces unnecessary repetition.
It also makes your stylesheet easier to read.

blocks.title: Another Group
blocks.output: Both classes receive the same margin and font weight.

blocks.text: Grouping is especially useful when several elements share foundational styling.

blocks.question: What does the comma do in h1, h2, h3 { color: black; }?
options: It makes h2 a child of h1.
It combines the three elements into one HTML element.
It groups the selectors so they share the declarations.
It makes the selector more specific than an ID.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Commas group selectors that should share the same declarations.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about why three selectors appear before one declaration block.
blocks.reasoning: The comma allows multiple independent selectors to use the same CSS declaration block.

blocks.text: Descendant Selectors
Now we are going to make our selectors more precise.
Imagine that your page contains many paragraphs.
You may want to style only the paragraphs inside a particular card.

blocks.title: Nested HTML
blocks.code:
Account

Balance: GHS 250

This paragraph is outside the card.
blocks.output: The page contains a card with a paragraph and another paragraph outside the card.

blocks.text: A simple p selector would target both paragraphs.
But we only want the paragraph inside the card.
A descendant selector can solve this.

blocks.title: Descendant Selector
blocks.output: Only p elements inside .card are targeted.

blocks.text: The space between .card and p is important.
It means select p elements that are descendants of an element with the card class.
The paragraph does not need to be a direct child.
It can exist deeper inside the card and still match the selector.

blocks.title: Deeper Descendant
blocks.output: The paragraph is still a descendant of .card.

blocks.text: The selector .card p can still target this paragraph.

blocks.question: What does .card p target?
options: Only elements with both card and p classes
Every p element on the page
p elements that are descendants of .card
Only the first p directly inside .card
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The space creates a descendant relationship.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Focus on what the space between the two selectors means.
blocks.reasoning: .card p targets paragraph elements located anywhere inside an element with class card.

blocks.text: Child Selectors
Sometimes the descendant selector is too broad.
You may want to target only elements that are direct children of another element.
CSS provides the greater-than symbol for this purpose.

blocks.title: Direct Child Selector
blocks.output: Only p elements that are direct children of .card are targeted.

blocks.text: The greater-than symbol means direct child.
This is different from the normal descendant selector.

blocks.title: Direct Child Versus Nested Element
blocks.output:
The first paragraph is a direct child of .card.
The second paragraph is nested inside .content.

blocks.text: With .card > p, only the first paragraph matches.
With .card p, both paragraphs match.
That small symbol changes the meaning of the selector significantly.

blocks.question: Which selector targets only direct p children of .card?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The > combinator targets direct children.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the selector combinator that specifically means direct child.
blocks.reasoning: .card > p matches p elements whose immediate parent is an element with class card.

blocks.text: Attribute Selectors
Selectors can also target elements based on their HTML attributes.
This becomes useful when working with forms, links, inputs and reusable components.

blocks.title: Form Inputs
blocks.code:
<input type="text" placeholder="Username">
<input type="email" placeholder="Email">
<input type="password" placeholder="Password">
blocks.output: The page contains three different input types.

blocks.text: Suppose we want to style every text input.
We can use an attribute selector.

blocks.title: Attribute Selector
blocks.output: Only the input whose type attribute is text receives these styles.

blocks.text: The square brackets contain the attribute condition.
Here we are asking CSS to find input elements whose type attribute equals text.
This lets us target elements based on information already present in their HTML.

blocks.title: Styling Email Inputs
blocks.output: Only email inputs receive the blue border color.

blocks.text: Attribute selectors are particularly useful when an element type alone is not specific enough.

blocks.question: What does input[type="email"] target?
options: Every element with the email class
Every input regardless of its type
Input elements whose type attribute is email
Only elements whose ID is email
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The selector checks the input element's type attribute.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look carefully at the attribute condition inside the square brackets.
blocks.reasoning: input[type="email"] matches input elements where the type attribute has the value email.

blocks.text: Combining Selectors
Now let's combine the ideas you have learned.
Combining selectors allows you to create very precise targets.
For example, imagine that your application has many cards and each card has a title.

blocks.title: Targeting a Card Title
blocks.output: h2 elements inside dashboard-card elements receive the styles.

blocks.text: This selector is more specific than simply using h2.
It says that we want h2 elements inside dashboard cards.
Now imagine a special card that should have a different title.

blocks.title: Special Card
blocks.output: The card has both dashboard-card and featured classes.

blocks.text: We can target an element that has both classes by writing the class selectors without a space.

blocks.title: Two Classes on the Same Element
blocks.output: Only elements containing both dashboard-card and featured are targeted.

blocks.text: This is different from .dashboard-card .featured.
Without a space, both classes must belong to the same element.
With a space, the second selector represents a descendant inside the first selector.

blocks.question: What does .dashboard-card.featured select?
options: A featured element anywhere inside dashboard-card
Elements that have both dashboard-card and featured classes
Every dashboard-card and every featured element
Only featured elements that are direct children of dashboard-card
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Without a space, both classes must match the same element.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Pay attention to the absence of a space between the two class selectors.
blocks.reasoning: .dashboard-card.featured requires one element to have both classes.

blocks.text: Specificity: When Rules Compete
Now we need to understand what happens when more than one CSS rule targets the same element.
This situation happens frequently in real projects.
CSS has a system called specificity that helps determine which competing selector has greater priority.
For our beginner foundation, remember the general order from lower to higher specificity.
Element selectors are generally less specific than class selectors.
Class selectors are generally less specific than ID selectors.

blocks.title: Specificity Example
blocks.output: A paragraph with class note and ID special-note is targeted by multiple rules.

blocks.text: If one paragraph has the ID special-note and the class note, all three selectors can potentially match it.
The ID selector has greater specificity than the class and element selectors in this simple comparison.
This is why understanding selectors helps you understand why a style appears to win over another style.
Do not try to solve every CSS conflict by adding more selectors randomly.
First inspect which rules are matching the element.
Then think about specificity and the order in which the rules appear.

blocks.question: In this simple comparison, which selector generally has greater specificity?
options: All three always have equal specificity
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. An ID selector generally has greater specificity than a class or element selector.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Recall the basic specificity order introduced in this lesson.
blocks.reasoning: In the basic comparison, ID selectors have greater specificity than class selectors, which have greater specificity than element selectors.

blocks.text: Build a Dashboard Interface
Now we are going to use selectors in something closer to a real application.
Imagine you are building a user dashboard.
The dashboard contains a header, navigation links, cards and buttons.
Start with this HTML.

blocks.title: Dashboard HTML
blocks.code:
My Dashboard

Welcome back.

Overview Projects Settings

Projects

You have 8 active projects.

Learning Progress

You completed 72% of your current course.
blocks.output: A basic dashboard structure is displayed with a header, navigation and two cards.

blocks.text: Before styling anything, inspect the class names.
The dashboard uses classes to identify reusable components.
The featured card has two classes because it is both a dashboard card and a special featured card.
Now let's use selectors to style different parts of the dashboard.

blocks.title: Dashboard Base Selectors
blocks.output: The dashboard receives a base font, the header becomes dark and the title receives specific styling.

blocks.text: Notice how each selector has a different job.
The dashboard class targets the overall application area.
The dashboard-header class targets the header component.
The dashboard-title ID targets the particular main title.

blocks.title: Navigation Selectors
blocks.output: The navigation receives a background, its links receive shared styling and the active link receives a special style.

blocks.text: Look at the selector .dashboard-nav .nav-link.
It targets nav-link elements that are descendants of dashboard-nav.
Now look at .dashboard-nav .nav-link.active.
The active class is attached to the same link element as nav-link.
That selector therefore targets only navigation links that are active.

blocks.title: Dashboard Cards
blocks.output: The dashboard cards receive shared styling and their headings and paragraphs receive targeted styles.

blocks.text: Notice that .dashboard-card h2 does not style every h2 on the page.
It only targets h2 elements inside dashboard cards.
This is how selector combinations help you control larger interfaces.

blocks.title: Featured Card Selector
blocks.output: Only the featured dashboard card receives the stronger border and blue heading.

blocks.text: Now the special card can look different without creating an entirely separate card system.
This is a practical example of combining reusable classes with specific selectors.

blocks.question: Which selector targets only h2 elements inside elements that have both dashboard-card and featured classes?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The two classes without a space must match the same element, followed by h2 inside it.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Pay close attention to whether there is a space between the two class selectors.
blocks.reasoning: .dashboard-card.featured h2 means an h2 descendant of an element that has both classes.

blocks.text: Selector Practice Challenge
Now I want you to reason about selectors before choosing your answer.
Do not choose an option simply because it looks familiar.
Look carefully at the symbols and spaces.

blocks.question:
Given

Text

, which selector targets the paragraph inside the card?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The space creates a descendant relationship.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Check the difference between selecting two classes and selecting a descendant.
blocks.reasoning: .card p selects p elements that are descendants of an element with class card.

blocks.question:
Given

Text

, which selector still targets the paragraph?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The paragraph is a descendant of card even though it is not a direct child.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The paragraph is nested one level deeper, so think about descendant selection.
blocks.reasoning: .card p can target descendants at any depth, while .card > p requires a direct child relationship.

blocks.question: Given <button class="btn primary">Save</button>, which selector targets this exact class combination?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Without a space, both classes must belong to the same element.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Remember that a space means descendant, while no space means the same element has both classes.
blocks.reasoning: .btn.primary matches an element that contains both btn and primary classes.

blocks.question: Which selector targets input elements whose type is password?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. This is an attribute selector.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the selector that checks the type attribute.
blocks.reasoning: input[type="password"] selects input elements where the type attribute equals password.

blocks.question: Which selector targets only direct paragraph children of .content?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The > symbol means direct child.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The question says direct children, so look for the direct-child combinator.
blocks.reasoning: .content > p matches p elements whose immediate parent is .content.

blocks.text: Your Selector Thinking Process
You now know many selector types, but memorizing symbols is not enough.
You need a reliable process for choosing the right selector.
First ask what element you actually want to style.
Next ask whether the target should be reusable.
If it represents a reusable component or category, a class is often appropriate.
If you need a particular unique element, an ID can identify it.
If you want every element of a particular HTML type, an element selector may be enough.
If the element needs to be identified by where it sits inside another component, use a relationship selector.
If the element needs to be identified by an HTML attribute, consider an attribute selector.
The goal is not to create the longest selector possible.
The goal is to create a selector that targets exactly what you mean without unnecessary complexity.
That is an important habit for professional CSS development.

blocks.question: You have 20 buttons that should share the same design. Which approach is generally the most reusable?
options: Give every button a unique ID and style each one separately.
Use the button element selector for every possible button style.
Give the buttons a shared class and style that class.
Use an attribute selector for every button regardless of its attributes.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A reusable class is usually the cleanest solution for shared component styling.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about which selector is specifically designed to be reused across many elements.
blocks.reasoning: A shared class allows many elements to receive the same component styling from one rule.

blocks.text: Final Selector Test
This final section checks whether you can actually reason about selectors.
Read each question carefully before choosing an option.
Pay special attention to dots, hashes, spaces, commas and greater-than symbols.

blocks.question: Which selector targets every element with class="card"?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. .card targets elements with the card class.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Remember that reusable classes are selected with a dot.
blocks.reasoning: A class selector uses a dot followed by the class name.

blocks.question: Which selector targets every h2 inside .card, including deeply nested h2 elements?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The descendant selector can match nested elements at any depth.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The question allows deeply nested elements, so a direct-child selector is too restrictive.
blocks.reasoning: .card h2 targets h2 descendants anywhere inside .card.

blocks.question: Which selector targets h2 only when it is a direct child of .card?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The > combinator means direct child.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the selector that restricts the relationship to an immediate parent.
blocks.reasoning: .card > h2 requires the h2 to have .card as its immediate parent.

blocks.question: Which selector targets an element that has both classes button and active?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. No space means both classes are on the same element.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: A space changes the relationship to descendant, so look for the option without a space.
blocks.reasoning: .button.active matches one element containing both class names.

blocks.question: Which selector targets all links inside .navigation that also have the active class?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. a.active targets active links, and the navigation selector limits them to links inside .navigation.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The active class belongs to the link itself, so the class selector should be attached to a.
blocks.reasoning: .navigation a.active means an a element with class active that is a descendant of .navigation.

blocks.question: Which selector is an attribute selector for text inputs?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The selector checks the input element's type attribute.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: An attribute selector uses square brackets around the attribute condition.
blocks.reasoning: input[type="text"] targets input elements whose type attribute equals text.

blocks.text: Lesson Complete
You have completed CSS Selectors.
You now understand that selectors are the targeting system of CSS.
You learned how element selectors target HTML elements.
You learned how class selectors create reusable styling targets.
You learned how ID selectors identify particular elements.
You learned how multiple classes can work together on one element.
You learned how commas can group selectors.
You learned how spaces create descendant relationships.
You learned how the greater-than symbol targets direct children.
You learned how attribute selectors can target elements based on their HTML attributes.
You also received your first introduction to CSS specificity.
Most importantly, you used these selectors to style a dashboard-like interface.
From this point forward, do not look at a selector as a strange collection of symbols.
Read it as a sentence describing exactly what CSS should target.
In the next lesson, we will use CSS selectors to control colors, backgrounds and borders in much greater detail.
